text: The purest ABF-film and copper-resin adhesion chokepoints appear concentrated in non-US primary listings: Ajinomoto for ABF and MEC Company for copper surface treatment/adhesion chemistry. US-listed candidates are mostly adjacent yield-enablers or direct customers.

MKSI should be carried forward as the strongest US-exchange underfollowed candidate for substrate chemistry/equipment because Atotech directly touches package substrate manufacturing, copper plating, ABF-compatible processes, and electronics packaging.

ONTO and CAMT should be carried forward as yield-enabler candidates rather than materials suppliers; their survival depends on proving advanced packaging/substrate inspection revenue is material and growing with AI package complexity.

AMKR is a reference demand-pull platform for FCBGA and advanced packaging. It is useful for tracking substrate procurement constraints, but it is less directly tied to the upstream material chokepoint than MKSI, ONTO, or CAMT.

For advanced-package substrates, the key bottleneck signal from supplied evidence is beneath finished substrate makers: ABF build-up insulating film and copper-bonding / surface-chemistry inputs may be more concentrated and harder to substitute than substrate capacity alone.

US-listed pure-play exposure to ABF film and copper-bonding surface chemistry appears limited; best Layer 1B US-listed candidates may be adjacent materials, process-chemistry, and packaging-equipment companies requiring primary-source verification.

Prioritize deeper verification on MKSI / Atotech for IC substrate metallization, electroless copper, electroplating, and surface-treatment exposure, because this maps most directly to the copper-adhesion chokepoint in the supplied evidence.

ENTG and KLIC remain underfollowed US-listed hypotheses rather than confirmed node beneficiaries until filings or product literature show direct advanced-packaging substrate, ABF, FC-BGA, or OSAT/customer exposure.

ESI should be prioritized for later-layer verification because MacDermid Alpha has explicit IC substrate copper plating, copper adhesion, surface finish, RDL, panel-level packaging, and SAP exposure while ESI remains within the preferred mid-cap hunting range.

MKSI is a larger but still relevant proxy through Atotech; next work should isolate Atotech electronics/package-substrate revenue and determine whether AI/HPC substrate capacity expansions flow through MKS chemistry, equipment, or software.
CAMT is not a substrate-material supplier but may be a yield-gate candidate for advanced packaging inspection/metrology; keep as hypothesis until substrate/RDL/customer specificity is proven.

For US-listed assets, the cleanest investable mapping may be process chemistry and inspection/metrology rather than ABF film itself, because the supplied context identifies non-US or not-cleanly-US-listed leaders at the deepest build-up film and copper-bonding layers.

Layer 2 should test whether these names are genuinely underfollowed AI infrastructure beneficiaries or simply already priced specialty-materials/equipment stories by checking analyst coverage, AI/advanced-packaging revenue contribution, and management commentary frequency.

MKSI should be tracked as a US-listed Atotech proxy for IC-substrate wet chemistry, surface treatment, metallization, and plating exposure; verify actual AI/HPC substrate revenue contribution before upgrading.
CAMT is the cleanest under-USD-10B US-listed discovery candidate found in this pass for advanced packaging yield/metrology exposure, with recent OSAT orders tied to CoWoS-like AI packaging.

ENTG maps to substrate integrity, contamination control, materials handling, Cu plating deposition integrity, and yield in advanced packaging, but its revenue exposure to this exact node needs quantification.
DD has credible advanced IC-substrate materials exposure through interconnect, dry film photoresist, and copper chemistry, but corporate-separation and segment-mix verification are required.

The most direct ABF film and copper-adhesion chokepoints appear to be non-US or not cleanly investable as US-listed small/mid-cap equities; US-listed mapping is mostly through adjacent chemistry, materials handling, and inspection/metrology suppliers.

US-listed pure-play merchant suppliers of high-end sub-100nm barium titanate powder appear scarce; key powder names found in evidence are mostly Japan/China listings or private entities such as Ferro/Vibrantz.

VSH and KN are the best current US-listed underfollowed discovery-lane candidates, but both are MLCC/ceramic capacitor product hypotheses rather than confirmed high-end BaTiO3 powder chokepoint beneficiaries.
MRAAY and TTDKY should be retained as reference leaders for AI-server MLCC demand validation, not as underfollowed alpha candidates.
Next layer should separately map non-US direct powder suppliers: Sakai Chemical, Nippon Chemical Industrial, Fuji Titanium, Shandong Sinocera, and private Vibrantz/Ferro.

Sakai Chemical / SACIF should be promoted to a focused Layer 2 verification target for AI-server MLCC upstream dielectric powder exposure, with emphasis on BaTiO3 share, nano-hydrothermal capability, capacity, and customer evidence.

Nippon Chemical Industrial / NPNHF is a speculative shadow candidate due to official barium-carbonate-to-BaTiO3-for-MLCC product evidence, but US OTC ticker/liquidity and revenue materiality must be verified before inclusion in a stronger universe.

The strongest current fact pattern is downstream demand pull: Murata materials and industry reports support rising AI-server MLCC intensity; upstream powder tightness remains a hypothesis requiring supplier-level evidence.
US-listed pure-play access to high-end BaTiO3 dielectric powder appears limited; the practical US-accessible universe may rely on OTC Japanese listings plus reference ADRs for MLCC makers.

For the AI server MLCC dielectric-powder node, direct public-market exposure appears stronger in Japan-listed suppliers such as Sakai Chemical and Nippon Chemical Industrial than in clean US-listed names.
MTRN should enter the US-listed underfollowed watchlist as a hypothesis-only BaTiO3 specialty-materials candidate; survival requires proof of MLCC-grade commercial sales or capacitor-maker customers.
VSH is a second-order MLCC-component proxy, not an upstream dielectric-powder supplier; keep only if evidence appears for AI-server-qualified MLCC orders, pricing, or capacity tightness.
CBT is a stale-asset trail: historical Cabot barium titanate ceramics exposure exists, but the current product/business status must be confirmed before use in later Serenity layers.

The purest high-end BaTiO3 dielectric-powder suppliers for AI-server MLCCs appear to be non-US listed or private; US-listed exposure is mostly downstream MLCC makers, OTC ADRs, or adjacent passive-component suppliers.

Sakai Chemical 4078.JP should remain the key non-US upstream reference for future non-US universe expansion, but it should not be inserted into a US-listed candidate list unless a verifiable US-traded ordinary/ADR instrument is found.

For US-listed candidates, the correct falsification test is not simply MLCC exposure; it is evidence of high-capacitance/thin-layer MLCC demand, AI-server qualification, pricing power, capacity tightness, or dielectric-powder procurement constraints.

Vishay is the best-fit US-listed underfollowed candidate found in this pass, but its direct link to AI-server-grade thin-layer MLCCs and sub-100nm BaTiO3 powder is weak and must be treated as a hypothesis until product mix and customer exposure are verified.

POWL is the cleanest direct underfollowed US-listed candidate for data-center electrical power delivery in this pass because official 2026 releases explicitly connect record backlog and a $400M-plus order to data-center/AI power needs.

IESC should remain in the underfollowed lane as a data-center electrical/infrastructure execution beneficiary, but later layers must split data-center exposure from residential and other commercial construction exposure.
ATKR is a second-order cable-management/raceway/conduit beneficiary; exposure is plausible but less pure and needs product-level data-center revenue verification.

Hammond Power Solutions appears highly relevant for dry-type transformers and data-center backlog but is Canadian-listed rather than a primary US-listed company; evaluate separately if OTC/Canada-listed names are allowed in a later non-US pass.

Encore Wire would have been a strong US-listed cable candidate, but it became privately held after Prysmian completed the acquisition; use Prysmian only if ADR/non-US listings are permitted in a broader pass.

POWL is the cleanest direct US-listed underfollowed candidate for data-center electrical power delivery because company evidence ties it to a $400M-plus behind-the-meter data-center order and record backlog.
IESC is a strong execution-layer candidate: data-center infrastructure demand drove FY2025 Infrastructure Solutions growth and backlog expansion, but residential and other segments complicate purity.
ATKR remains a lower-confidence second-order candidate because it explicitly serves data-center electrical applications but still needs revenue-mix and backlog verification.
NVT is near the upper end of the hunting filter but has unusually relevant exposure to data-center electrical connection, protection, grounding, and power-distribution hardware.

The power-delivery chokepoint appears to include both hard goods and execution capacity: switchgear, power control rooms, conduit/cable management, connectors, grounding, enclosures, and qualified electrical project delivery.

Need a follow-up pass on US-listed transformer-specific names and regulated inputs such as transformer oil, copper/aluminum conductor capacity, specialty steel, and testing/certification bottlenecks; this pass found stronger evidence for switchgear and electrical execution than for transformer manufacturing.
POWL should be tracked as a direct switchgear/packaged-power candidate for the data_center_power_delivery node; recent evidence includes record backlog and a >$400M data-center order.
IESC should be tracked as an underfollowed electrical-infrastructure execution candidate; the key verification issue is how much backlog is truly data-center-driven and enforceable.
NVT belongs in the discovery lane despite larger market cap because Avail EPG adds switchgear, bus systems and control-building exposure that maps directly to power-delivery bottlenecks.
ATKR is a weaker, second-order conduit/cable-management hypothesis; retain for Layer 2 only if data-center revenue mix, backlog or distributor demand can be verified.
Need a separate cable/conductor pass for still-listed US or ADR names after Encore Wire's delisting; many pure cable assets are now private, foreign-listed, or absorbed by larger strategic buyers.

POWL should be tracked as a direct switchgear/power-control-room candidate for AI data-center electrical power delivery; strongest next check is backlog composition and data-center award repeatability.

IESC should be tracked as an underfollowed project-execution/electrical-contracting beneficiary; verify data-center customer mix, Communications segment growth, RPO quality, and labor/capacity constraints.

ATKR should be tracked as a cable-management/conduit hypothesis rather than a proven chokepoint; require evidence that data-center demand is material enough to offset cyclical electrical-products weakness.
nVent is useful as a non-mega reference for electrical connection/protection exposure to AI data centers and power utilities, but it is less obscure than the main discovery lane.
Need a separate pass on US-listed or OTC transformer manufacturers and foreign ADR/OTC suppliers, because many pure transformer assets appear private, non-US-listed, or foreign-listed.

BELFB should remain in the underfollowed discovery lane for thermal/power-conditioning component research; verify AI server/data-center power design wins and whether revenue is material enough to survive Layer 2.

NVT is a direct rack-level AI power/cooling infrastructure candidate, but market cap and rising AI attention mean it should be treated as a quality reference-plus-discovery bridge rather than a deeply obscure small-cap.

MOD is a direct data-center thermal-management candidate with filings evidence for CDUs and immersion solutions; next layer should test whether data-center growth offsets legacy thermal/HVAC exposure.

The thermal_and_power_conditioning_components node maps cleanly into CDUs, manifolds, heat exchangers, rear-door coolers, chillers, immersion systems, smart PDUs, front-end power supplies, magnetic components, circuit protection, connectors and UPS/battery assets.

Need a follow-up pass specifically for lower-level pump, valve, sensor, coolant/fluid, busbar, connector, and power-module suppliers; current pass found direct public names but not enough hard supplier-customer evidence below the rack/system layer.

NVT should remain on the thermal_and_power_conditioning_components watchlist as a high-purity but no-longer-small-cap underfollowed candidate: liquid cooling plus rack power distribution maps directly to AI rack density.
VICR should be tracked as a power-conditioning component candidate; survival depends on evidence of AI/HPC design wins, volume conversion, and customer concentration risk.
BELFB is a lower-attention component hypothesis for data-center power, protection, magnetics, and connectivity; it requires segment/order evidence before moving beyond Layer 1.
MOD was identified in search as a relevant data-center cooling supplier and should be evaluated in a separate thermal-focused pass; it was excluded here only due to the four-candidate cap.

Reference leaders such as VRT should be used to map downward into qualified subcomponents: CDUs, manifolds, busway, PDUs, power modules, magnetics, connectors, leak detection, filtration, and controls.

NVT is a high-relevance liquid-cooling and rack-power reference candidate for AI racks; despite large-cap size, its CDUs, manifolds, PDUs, NVIDIA/Siemens reference links, and disclosed liquid-cooling deployment base make it useful as a benchmark for smaller thermal/power candidates.

MOD has unusually direct data-center cooling evidence, including a USD 4B long-term Airedale capacity agreement through 2029, CDU products, immersion-cooling IP, and a new Data Centers reporting segment; verify customer concentration and margins.

POWL is a power-conditioning/switchgear second-order candidate for AI campuses; evidence supports exposure to data-center/AI-driven medium-voltage opportunities, but order lumpiness and backlog mix must be verified before upgrading confidence.

BELFB is a lower-attention component hypothesis for data-center power conversion via 48V power supplies and power shelves; needs hard evidence of AI-server design wins, hyperscaler qualification, and revenue mix.

For high-density AI racks, the chokepoint may split into two coupled subnodes: thermal loops/CDUs/manifolds/chillers and power path components/switchgear/48V conversion/PDUs. Qualification, uptime requirements, and reference architectures create potential switching costs.

Next Layer 1C should search for US-listed and ADR suppliers of pumps, valves, heat exchangers, sensors, specialty coolants, busbars, and certification/testing providers; current pass found stronger evidence in system/subsystem vendors than in pure component suppliers.
MOD should remain in the thermal-management discovery lane because it has hard order evidence from an AI infrastructure developer via Airedale data-center cooling systems.

NVT should remain in the component/subsystem discovery lane because it maps directly to CDUs, coolant manifolds, rear-door heat exchangers, racks, and high-density PDUs rather than only branded data-center integration.
POWL should remain in the power-conditioning discovery lane because behind-the-meter data-center power orders create a measurable signal for switchgear and packaged electrical infrastructure demand.

VRT is useful as a reference anchor, but later layers should map Vertiv downward into suppliers of cooling modules, pumps, heat exchangers, controls, power electronics, busbars, switchgear, sensors, and qualified manufacturing capacity.

Current market-cap buckets were not verified from a dedicated live market-cap source in this pass; later dashboard enrichment should attach market cap, liquidity, analyst coverage, and revenue mix before scoring.
CRWV should be retained as the reference public specialized AI cloud capacity leader, not as the underfollowed alpha target.
NBIS is a direct AI cloud capacity candidate; verify ARR quality, customer concentration, data-center power availability, and financing before promotion beyond Layer 1.

IREN is a strong underfollowed-lane candidate because it combines AI cloud GPU capacity with legacy crypto-infrastructure perception; key risks are execution, financing, dilution, and customer concentration.
APLD is a speculative shadow candidate for AI data-center capacity rather than pure GPU cloud; prioritize verification of contracted MW, tenant credit, energization schedule, and project financing.

TeraWulf and Cipher appear relevant for a separate colocation / power-secured data-center capacity pass, but were not included in the four-name candidate limit because this pass prioritizes direct specialized AI cloud and obvious capacity platforms.
CRWV should remain the reference benchmark for specialized AI cloud capacity, but its high attention and large market cap mean it should not dominate the underfollowed discovery lane.

IREN has become a direct AI cloud capacity candidate because of disclosed NVIDIA/Microsoft-linked GPU cloud contracts and secured-power expansion claims; key risk is execution, financing, and concentration.
APLD maps to the power-to-AI-factory infrastructure layer rather than pure GPU cloud ownership; verify leases, tenant quality, project finance, and delivery milestones.

BTDR is a speculative shadow candidate: strong power-site optionality and early AI cloud disclosures, but AI revenue and customer proof need much stronger verification before advancing to later Serenity layers.

Potential next-pass names not included due to 4-candidate limit: HUT, WULF, NBIS, and possibly CORZ depending on CoreWeave transaction status and listing availability. These should be checked in a follow-up infrastructure/conversion pass.

Keep CRWV as the high-attention category benchmark for specialized AI cloud capacity; use it to compare backlog quality, utilization, financing, and customer concentration of smaller AI/HPC capacity pivots.

IREN should remain in the universe as a direct AI cloud capacity candidate, but later layers must verify actual deployed GPUs, contracted utilization, customer concentration, and financing terms because the model is capex-intensive.

APLD belongs in the discovery lane as a messy-label AI data-center capacity candidate; survival depends on lease commencement, tenant credit quality, power availability, and economics after debt service.
CIFR is a speculative-shadow candidate because the market may still classify it as a bitcoin miner while disclosed agreements suggest a transition toward HPC capacity leasing.

WULF and NBIS were not included in the four-candidate list but should be retained for the broader node watchlist: WULF as a mining-to-HPC capacity pivot, NBIS as a now high-attention neocloud reference with large customer agreements.

The key research variable for this node is not announced GPU count alone; it is billable capacity with secured power, cooling, networking, financing, construction execution, and durable customer commitments.
CoreWeave should remain the reference benchmark for specialized AI cloud capacity, but not dominate underfollowed discovery because it is now high-attention and large-cap.
Applied Digital is a second-order capacity candidate where the primary chokepoint is power-ready AI/HPC colocation leased to neocloud customers, especially CoreWeave.
IREN is a shadow-capacity candidate because legacy bitcoin-mining infrastructure, secured power, and self-owned data centers may be repurposed into AI cloud GPU services.
Nebius is a direct neocloud candidate with dedicated GPU cluster contracts; further work should stress-test customer concentration, capex funding, and utilization.
Layer 2 should verify which candidates have binding customer contracts versus illustrative ARR targets, and should separate contracted megawatts from speculative power pipeline.

TENB is a direct Layer 1B candidate for critical-infrastructure cybersecurity automation because Tenable has explicit OT Security, cyber-physical asset discovery, and IT/OT exposure-management positioning.

DGII is a strong underfollowed candidate because it sits in secure industrial IoT, data-center/edge remote access, out-of-band management, and cloud-based device-management workflows rather than mainstream cybersecurity screens.

BDC is a plausible shadow beneficiary for OT data, industrial networking, security, and data-center/smart-building connectivity; later layers must separate security/software exposure from legacy cable/connectivity exposure.

The node is likely less about broad cybersecurity spend and more about embedded identity, OT asset discovery, secure remote access, and automation workflows in environments where outages are costly and switching costs are high.
Layer 1C should verify revenue purity: OT/security/data-center automation may be a small portion of each candidate's revenue, especially for BDC and DGII.
TENB should remain a reference candidate for OT cybersecurity exposure, but later layers must isolate whether OT Security is material inside the broader exposure-management platform.

DGII is a promising underfollowed candidate because secure industrial IoT connectivity, Opengear out-of-band management, and recurring remote-management software sit one layer beneath obvious cybersecurity vendors.

BDC is an underfollowed infrastructure/software hybrid candidate: industrial networking and OT cybersecurity may benefit from critical-infrastructure automation, but software/security materiality must be verified.
ITRI is a grid-edge utility workflow hypothesis. The thesis depends on software/services mix and regulated-utility switching costs, not generic smart-meter hardware demand.

Private OT secure-access vendors such as Xona, Dispel, Secomea, and OPSWAT appear highly relevant but are not US-listed pure-play candidates; they should be used as category-validation comps rather than stock candidates.

The likely chokepoint is not endpoint cybersecurity alone; it is certified, auditable, low-disruption access and automation across legacy OT assets where uptime and regulatory compliance constrain vendor substitution.
TENB is the public reference anchor for OT cybersecurity; many cleaner OT pure plays are private, so Tenable can be used to benchmark public-market multiples, product language, and customer evidence.
ITRI should be tracked as a hidden utility-grid operations software candidate rather than a pure cybersecurity company; key validation is recurring software/services mix and grid-edge/DERMS adoption.
DGII is a narrow secure industrial connectivity and remote infrastructure-management candidate; key validation is software/service attach rate and utility/energy customer evidence.
PD is a weaker but relevant second-order cloud/data-center operations automation candidate; survival depends on proof that AI/cloud complexity is improving retention and automation usage.

Private OT cybersecurity leaders including Dragos, Claroty, Nozomi, and Armis create a public-market mapping gap; future layers should compare public candidates against these private benchmarks without treating private-company attention as investable evidence.

TENB should be carried forward as the most direct underfollowed public-market mapping for OT cybersecurity tied to AI data-center and critical-infrastructure exposure; key survival test is whether OT Security revenue/materiality can be verified.

ITRI is an adjacent automation candidate, not a pure cybersecurity name. It belongs in the node only if grid-edge software, DERMS, managed services or utility operations workflows show recurring revenue and switching-cost evidence.
BDC is a hardware/software hybrid OT-networking candidate; underfollowed angle depends on proving industrial cybersecurity licensing and IT/OT convergence are material rather than marketing language.

The critical-infrastructure cybersecurity chokepoint appears to split into three subnodes: OT exposure/asset management, utility/grid automation workflows, and privileged/machine identity for hybrid cloud and regulated infrastructure.

Several strong OT secure-remote-access vendors found in search, including Xona, Dispel, Netop, TDi Technologies and OPSWAT, appear private or not cleanly US-listed; later layers should map public acquirers, distributors or embedded partners.

Technology theme should be decomposed into AI demand, HBM, advanced packaging, substrate yield, ABF film, copper-bonding chemistry, inspection/metrology, MLCC powders, optical connectivity, specialty foundry, data-center power, cooling, OT security, and secure infrastructure operations.

Highest initial bottleneck scores belong to ABF insulating film, copper-to-substrate surface chemistry, sub-100nm barium titanate dielectric powders, customer qualification gates, and advanced substrate yield.
Yield-driven constraints are more attractive for Serenity mapping than simple volume growth because they can protect incumbents through process know-how, customer qualification, and learning curves.
Do not allow GPU designers, cloud platforms, or obvious HBM producers to dominate the map; use them as demand/reference leaders and search one to two layers beneath them.

Near-term catalysts to track include HBM capacity commentary, substrate yield and customer-prepayment disclosures, MLCC material lead-time commentary, silicon-photonics customer wins, data-center electrical backlog, cooling capacity agreements, and OT cybersecurity attach rates.
Need primary-source verification for Ajinomoto ABF share, MEC surface-chemistry share, Sakai barium titanate share, and company-level revenue exposure for each mapped supplier.

Need filings and earnings-call checks for underfollowed nodes: Camtek OSAT/HBM order conversion, Element Solutions substrate chemistry exposure, Powell data-center backlog repeatability, Modine customer concentration, nVent data-center mix, Tenable OT module contribution, Digi ARR mix, Belden OT security attach rate, and IES data-center earnings contribution.

Policy and permitting events around grid interconnection, power availability, energy efficiency, water use, and critical-infrastructure cybersecurity could shift bottleneck value toward electrical, thermal, and OT security nodes.

POWL should be tracked as an underfollowed data-center power-delivery and switchgear candidate; survival to Layer 3 requires proof of repeatable AI/hyperscale data-center backlog, customer diversification, capacity execution, and margin discipline.

TENB should be tracked as an underfollowed OT/exposure-management candidate tied to AI-era critical infrastructure, but the relationship remains a hypothesis until OT Security revenue, attach rate, and utility/data-center customer evidence are quantified.

CAMT should be tracked as a higher-quality underfollowed advanced-packaging inspection/metrology relationship because Layer 2A evidence identifies yield as a key constraint in FC-BGA and advanced substrates.

ESI should remain a watch-list hypothesis for electronics materials and substrate process chemistry; confirm whether MacDermid Alpha has material AI/HPC substrate, FC-BGA, ABF, or advanced-packaging exposure.

MOD should be tracked as an AI data-center thermal-management candidate; survival requires primary-source validation of capacity-agreement quality, customer concentration, binding terms, and cooling-segment margin profile.
DGII should remain a lower-confidence underfollowed secure infrastructure monitoring candidate; verify ARR mix, Opengear/Lighthouse traction, and data-center or utility customer evidence.
NVT should be tracked as a large-cap but still potentially underappreciated AI infrastructure components supplier spanning enclosures, connections, power distribution, and liquid cooling.
TTDKY is a reference leader for validating AI-server MLCC and dielectric-powder constraints, not an underfollowed alpha candidate in this chunk.

BDC should remain a lower-confidence industrial networking and OT cybersecurity hypothesis; verify software/security attach rates and exposure to utilities, data centers, transit, and process automation.

Need primary-source filings, earnings calls, investor presentations, customer announcements, and segment-level data for all tickers in this chunk before upgrading relationships from hypothesis/inference to fact.

Need market-pricing checks for POWL, TENB, CAMT, ESI, MOD, DGII, NVT, TTDKY, and BDC: market cap, analyst count, revenue multiple, recent performance, short interest, estimate revisions, and whether the AI-infrastructure angle is already consensus.

Need falsification plans by node: data-center capex slowdown, easing switchgear/cooling lead times, customer insourcing, margin compression, one-time backlog digestion, OT security budget delays, or advanced-packaging capacity normalization.
MRAAY should be retained as a reference MLCC demand anchor, not as an underfollowed candidate; use Murata commentary to validate whether AI-server MLCC content and supply prioritization are real.

SACIF maps to the upstream BaTiO3 dielectric powder node; it is a high-priority underfollowed hypothesis but needs primary-source validation of electronic materials revenue, high-end powder capacity, and AI-server MLCC demand linkage.
ONTO maps to advanced-packaging inspection/metrology if the substrate constraint is yield rather than throughput; next layer should verify advanced packaging mix and customer/order evidence.
BELFB maps to AI rack power-conditioning and component infrastructure, but current evidence is weak; require company-level proof of data-center or AI-server order contribution.
VICR maps to high-density AI rack power conversion; survival into later layers depends on evidence of accelerator/rack design wins converting into material revenue.
ITRI maps to grid automation and utility operating software as a second-order beneficiary of AI data-center load growth, not to direct cybersecurity product demand.
CRWV is a reference AI cloud capacity benchmark for comparing NBIS and IREN on utilization, contracted revenue, power access, financing risk, and customer concentration.
NBIS maps to underfollowed AI-cloud capacity and sovereign/enterprise AI infrastructure, but requires verification that ARR corresponds to durable utilization and deployed GPU capacity.

IREN maps to power-secured AI compute infrastructure as a high-risk conversion story from crypto-adjacent infrastructure to AI cloud; prioritize falsification checks on financing, energization, and contracted revenue conversion.
PANW should be retained only as a cybersecurity reference platform; do not let it crowd out smaller OT, identity, utility automation, and infrastructure-management names.

Primary-source validation is missing for most ticker-specific claims in this chunk, especially BELFB, VICR, ITRI, NBIS, IREN, and ONTO. Next layer should pull filings, earnings calls, investor decks, product/customer disclosures, and segment revenue.

Market-pricing checks remain missing: market cap, valuation, analyst count, recent performance, short interest, institutional ownership, and whether the underfollowed angle is already widely recognized.
APLD should remain in the underfollowed AI/HPC capacity lane, but only as a construction, financing, and customer-concentration diligence candidate rather than a clean compute supplier.
TSM should be retained as a reference anchor for CoWoS, advanced packaging, and substrate demand validation, not as an underfollowed candidate.
ENTG maps to the advanced packaging yield-control materials layer, but the AI/HPC packaging contribution must be sized before it can rank as a high-conviction bottleneck exposure.
DD is useful as a scaled electronics-materials reference, but diversified portfolio dilution and restructuring/spin-off effects must be checked before assigning investable purity.
CIFR and BTDR belong in speculative_shadow, not core underfollowed, until binding HPC/AI contracts, power-site suitability, financing, and recognized non-bitcoin revenue are verified.
VSH and KN are weak-evidence capacitor shadows; both require capacitor segment mix, MLCC quality tier, backlog, customer, and AI/data-center exposure validation.
ETN should be retained as the electrical power-delivery benchmark for validating whether smaller suppliers have real AI data-center bottleneck exposure.
PD is an indirect operations-resilience hypothesis; survival to later layers depends on proof that AI/cloud complexity is improving retention, usage, automation adoption, or enterprise expansion.

Primary-source evidence is still missing for all ticker-specific relationships in this chunk: latest filings, earnings transcripts, investor presentations, product disclosures, customer contracts, backlog data, capex commitments, and segment revenue mix must be gathered in Layer 2C or Layer 3.

Market-pricing checks are still missing: current market cap, valuation, analyst coverage, recent performance, short interest, and whether the underfollowed angle is already priced should be added before ranking.

KYOCY mapped to AI-server MLCC/specialty ceramic capacitor node as an underfollowed second-order hypothesis; key survival test is direct KYOCERA AVX evidence in AI accelerator boards, server power, networking, or hyperscaler-qualified MLCC supply chains.

MTRN mapped to upstream electronic-ceramic/dielectric-powder node as a weak underfollowed hypothesis; key survival test is proof of commercial BaTiO3 or comparable high-end MLCC powder products and capacitor-maker customers.
CBT mapped to MLCC dielectric-powder node only as speculative shadow; should be removed unless current retained barium-titanate/electronic-ceramics assets or successor economics are documented.
Need primary-source validation for all three tickers: annual reports, product catalogs, technical datasheets, patents, customer/design-win references, distributor lead times, and earnings commentary.

Need market-pricing checks for KYOCY, MTRN, and CBT: market cap, analyst coverage, AI/MLCC keyword frequency in filings and calls, relative performance since AI-server MLCC narrative surfaced, and whether any perceived hidden exposure is already priced.
